It's been about 9 months since Jon Gottfried and I did something that felt both crazy and necessary: we swapped jobs.

After more than a decade of building MLH from a few hundred developers into a community that reaches nearly one in three new CS grads in the US annually, we were facing classic founder burnout. The roles we had held for years started to feel stale, and our energy was waning. We needed a change.

So last October, we ran an experiment. I moved away from day-to-day CEO duties and embedded myself with our customers, focusing entirely on a new challenge: helping them leverage AI to create meaningful developer engagement. Jon stepped in to lead the areas I had been managing.

The result? It's been a total game-changer for both of us and for MLH. The new perspective has been invigorating, and honestly, it feels like day zero all over again.

I'm incredibly grateful to Jon for taking this leap with me, and to our amazing team and community for their trust and support through this transition.

For any other founders out there feeling stuck in a role you've had for a decade, maybe it's time to consider your own "Freaky Friday." It might be the best decision you ever make.

Our friend Annabel wrote a great piece with more details on our swap. You can read it here: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/annabelburba_ever-wish-you-could-switch-jobs-with-someone-activity-7357031603941900289-1CMi

draft:
Subject: Let's talk about our story

Hey team,

I came across this excellent article on product storytelling and wanted to share it with all of you. It's a quick but powerful read.

**Link:** [Pitching a Product Idea](https://medium.com/the-year-of-the-looking-glass/pitching-a-product-idea-7566dd85c745)

The core message really struck me: we need to focus on the narrative and the experience we create, not just list features. It made me think about how we describe what we do at MLH.

Instead of saying:
* "We offer a Hardware Lab with the latest tech."
* "We create content and workshops for students."
* "We award prizes to the best hacks."

We should be telling the story of the experience:
* "We give a hacker the thrilling, hands-on experience of building their first robot or stepping into a VR world they coded themselves."
* "We guide a developer through that 'aha!' moment when a complex new technology finally clicks."
* "We create that unforgettable moment of recognition on stage, validating a hacker's creativity in front of their peers."

I know we all have incredible insights and stories like these from our work with the community, but right now, they're often siloed within our individual teams.

My question for all of you is: **How can we get better at aggregating these learnings and stories?**

What's the best way for us to share these experiences internally so we can use them to improve our offerings and tell a more compelling story?

Would love to hear your ideas in a reply here.
final:
Subject: We need to tell MLH's story:

Hey, folks --

Read this when y'all have the chance: [https://medium.com/the-year-of-the-looking-glass/pitching-a-product-idea-7566dd85c745](https://medium.com/the-year-of-the-looking-glass/pitching-a-product-idea-7566dd85c745) _This_ is the type of story-driven product development and description I want to get us to.  We often talk about our products in terms of what the features are (hardware lab, content creation, awarding a prize).  It's way more powerful to talk about them from the experiential perspective though (access to a devices hackers can't afford, content that explains new technology the way hackers want to learn, recognition for spending the weekend hacking on a cool new API).

We've got a lot of great places to draw material from, but they are very siloed in each of our teams' domains.

The question is: **How can we aggregate what we are learning across all of these different channels and then use it to make our offering even better?**  Hope you enjoy the read and it inspires you in some way!
  
- Swift
